passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a new antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure in a randomized controlled trial. Eighty adults aged 45–65 with mild hypertension were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the drug (n=40) or placebo (n=40). Baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP) was recorded for all participants. After 12 weeks of daily dosing, SBP was measured again. Table 1 presents the mean SBP change (in mmHg) and standard deviation for each group. The drug group exhibited a mean reduction of 12.5 mmHg (SD 4.3), whereas the placebo group showed a mean reduction of 3.2 mmHg (SD 5.1). The between-group difference in mean SBP reduction was 9.3 mmHg (p < 0.001), and the researchers concluded that the drug significantly lowered SBP compared to placebo. The study also reported that 25% of drug recipients experienced mild dizziness, while 10% of placebo recipients reported the same symptom. No serious adverse events were noted. The trial was double-blind, with neither participants nor investigators aware of group assignments. Adherence was monitored via pill counts, achieving an average compliance rate of 92% in the drug arm and 94% in placebo. Secondary outcomes included diastolic blood pressure and heart rate, which showed parallel trends to systolic changes.
table_data:
Sample ID | Treatment | Mean SBP Change (mmHg) | SD
1 | Drug | 12.5 | 4.3
2 | Placebo | 3.2 | 5.1
stem: What was the mean reduction in systolic blood pressure in the drug group?
explanation: Table 1 lists the mean SBP change for the drug group as 12.5 mmHg.
trap: Picking the placebo-group value (3.2) or one of the SDs (4.3, 5.1) from the table instead of the drug group's mean change.

explanation: Random assignment reduces selection bias and balances confounders between groups.

stem: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the study results?

options.A: The drug causes a 12.5 mmHg drop in all patients.
options.B: The drug is superior to placebo.
options.C: The drug has mild dizziness side effects.
options.D: No serious adverse events were observed.

explanation: The mean reduction reflects an average; individual responses vary.
trap: Assuming the mean applies uniformly to every patient.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the results of this trial?

options.A: The drug should be used as first-line therapy for all hypertensive patients.
options.B: In adults aged 45-65 with mild hypertension, the drug lowered mean SBP more than placebo over 12 weeks, with dizziness reported more often on the drug.
options.D: The drug should replace all other antihypertensives.

explanation: Correct: Mean SBP fell 12.5 mmHg on the drug versus 3.2 mmHg on placebo, and dizziness was reported by 25% versus 10%; B states only what the trial showed. Why the others are wrong: A) one 12-week trial in mild hypertension cannot establish first-line use for all hypertensive patients. C) the drug lowered SBP more than placebo. D) the trial did not compare the drug with other antihypertensives, so replacement is unsupported.
trap: Overgeneralizing one short trial in mild hypertension into a recommendation for first-line use or replacement of other drugs.
